books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, A. Reform Movements in the Antebellum Period

stimulus.text:
Alcohol use in the United States, in gallons of absolute alcohol per person aged 15 and older:

| Year | Gallons per person |
| --- | --- |
| 1790 | 5.8 |
| 1830 | 7.1 |
| 1840–1860 | about 3.5 |

The American Temperance Society, founded in 1826, claimed 1.5 million members by 1835.
stimulus.source_note: Table figures from W. J. Rorabaugh's research on American alcohol consumption, as reported by the National Archives ('Spirited Republic'): 5.8 gallons in 1790, 7.1 in 1830, about 3.5 by 1840-1860, per person aged 15 and older. Membership figure from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.11, A.

source: original; stimulus table drawn from Rorabaugh / National Archives figures and Barron's
stem: Which of the following best explains why the temperance movement drew its largest following in the 1830s?

options.text: The Eighteenth Amendment had just banned alcohol nationwide
options.misconception: National prohibition came in 1919, almost a century later.

options.text: Most Americans had already stopped drinking entirely by 1830
options.misconception: The table shows drinking at its peak in 1830, not its end.

options.text: Drinking peaked, and its costs fell hardest on women and families
The movement was led mainly by German and Irish Catholic immigrants
options.misconception: German and Irish Catholic immigrants mostly opposed temperance, not led it.

rationales.A: The Eighteenth Amendment was ratified in 1919. The temperance movement of the 1830s was a century earlier.
rationales.B: The table shows 1830 as the peak of drinking, with 7.1 gallons per person. Americans had not stopped drinking; they were drinking more than ever.
rationales.C: Drinking peaked in 1830, and women saw the cost at home: wages spent in taverns and drunken abuse. That is why women filled the movement's ranks.
rationales.D: Catholic immigrants from Germany and Ireland generally opposed temperance. The movement was led by Protestant women of the middle and upper classes.
rationales.general:
1. Check the date. The movement grew when drinking stood at its peak, 7.1 gallons in 1830.
2. Ask who paid. Women watched husbands spend pay in taverns and come home drunk.
3. Match the followers. The people hurt most became the movement's largest following.
Background: By 1830 the average man drank almost ten gallons of hard liquor a year, plus about thirty gallons of beer, wine, and cider.
Remember: a reform movement grows where the pain is felt — find who pays the cost.
